shock_low.description: Optional: the milder end of the shock (same sign convention). Gives the band.

shock_high.description: Optional: the harsher end of the shock.

incremental_margin.description: How much of a dollar on that line reaches net income, 0–1. A pass-through fee line is high (0.6–0.9); a full-cost product line is near the segment margin; a hedged line is low.

persistence_quarters.description: How many quarters the shock lasts, 0.25–8 (capped at 4 in the math).

moved_pct.description: The excess move since the event in percent, vs SPY ("0.5% vs SPY" → 0.5). Omit if none was measured.

- Only what THEY said about themselves, as a lasting rule or preference — never your read of them, never this trade's levels or size (the build keeps those), never a mood.
- Never ask questions to fill it. Keep it the moment they say it, and say in a few words that you will remember.
- They take one back ("I do trade small caps now") → call it with `forget: true` and the words of the old note.

note.description: The fact, in a short third-person line, as the user put it: "never trades low-float names", "only trades the open". To take one back, the words of the note to remove.

forget.description: true when the user takes a fact back ("I do trade small caps now") — removes the note matching `note`.

analyst.name: consult
analyst.description:
Put ONE decision to a more capable desk head and get a straight answer back. It cannot see this conversation and cannot fetch anything — you hand it the question and every number it needs, and it thinks harder than you can in-line.

Reach for it in exactly three situations: **the price target you are about to publish** — our number against the Street IS the edge, so the multiple and the arithmetic behind it have to hold up to someone attacking them; **a variant perception you cannot separate from consensus** — the bull and bear cases read as evenly weighted and you must say which way the evidence actually leans rather than splitting the difference; and **two valuation methods that disagree materially** (a DCF against comps, say) where you have to decide which one governs the target and defend that choice.

Do NOT reach for it to look something up, to double-check work you are already confident in, to summarize, or because a question feels big. A consult costs a full model call and adds seconds to the turn: if you already know the answer, or a tool call would settle it, that is the cheaper and better move. Most turns should end without it.

context.description: Everything needed to answer it: the levels, the account size and risk rule, the two readings that disagree. The consulted desk head cannot see your conversation and cannot fetch anything, so whatever you leave out simply is not considered.

mentor.name: flip_test
mentor.description:
Have this plan's DIRECTION attacked by a second desk that cannot see your conversation. The server assembles the evidence itself — structure, levels, liquidity, imbalances, indicators, on the rung you name and on the daily — and a stronger model argues the opposite side from those numbers and returns a verdict: `stands` (the counter-case is weak), `two_sided` (the chart supports both about equally) or `reversed` (the numbers favour the other way).

You cannot influence what it is shown, which is the point: you supply only the ticker, the rung, the horizon and the direction already chosen. It has no macro read, no news and no catalyst calendar, so it must never be allowed to overrule a dated event.

Reach for it when the user ASKS for their direction challenged, and — once, at the moment a setup goes ready — when real money is behind it (a `live` or `manual` account). Never on paper unless asked, never twice on the same levels, and never on a plan the user brought unless they ask outright: taking someone's own plan down and then arguing with its direction is not what they came for.

timeframe.description: The rung the plan is DRAWN on (its premise timeframe). The daily is always included as well, whatever you name.

horizon.description: The trade's horizon, so the counter-case is argued over the same holding period.

direction.description: The direction the plan takes. The OTHER side is what gets argued.

mentor.description: Record the USER's sizing answer and get the server's figures back in the same turn. Call it the moment they give a size — "risk $1,000", "1%", "$20k position", "300 shares" — with their unit and their number, never yours ("never choose it for them"). It returns, per scenario, the quantity, the cash at risk, the position value and whether that fits the cash the account can deploy (with the largest size that does, when it does not); the money the trade pays and costs; and whether the Generate button is now lit. Read those out — do not recompute any of them. The answer is recorded as theirs and settles sizing by itself as soon as the stages before it are settled, so never ask for the size again after calling this. Call it again only when they CHANGE the size.

unit.description: The unit the USER sized in: risk in cash, risk as % of the account, position value in cash, position value as % of the account, or a number of shares/units.

value.description: Their number, in that unit — 1000 for "risk $1k", 1 for "1%".

multiplier.description: Contract or point value — futures and FX only. Omit for shares, ETFs and crypto.

mentor.name: get_price_structure
mentor.description: The `thesis` lens's chart facts, on the hour (a day trade: intraday · day — no break candidate, no heavy days), day (swing) or week (long-term) chart: the confirmed swings with their dates, the normal daily move (ATR), WHO IS IN CONTROL (buyers since a close over the last swing high, sellers since a close under the last swing low) and the context of the last break (reversal · continuation · breakout), the last fall (its start and its low), the heavy-volume days of the last 60 sessions, and CANDIDATE levels from the tested rule — the stop under the sellers' last swing, a deeper one under the whole fall (with the last date price traded under it), the target at the start of the fall (or a measured move at the highs) — and the BREAK CANDIDATE (the nearest high over the price, which a day close over arms scenario B; B's ASSUMED stop, target and context). The candidates are a starting point: judge the stop and the targets yourself against the chart and the candles, and say where you differ and why.

timeframe.description: The chart the trade is drawn on: `hour` for a day trade (intraday · day — the session's closed 1-hour bars), `day` for a swing, `week` for a long-term trade (bigger swings, a bigger stop and target).

side.description: Read for a long (default) or a short — a short reads the chart upside down: its stop over the buyers' last swing up.

mentor.name: get_entry_level
mentor.description: The `thesis` lens's entry arithmetic. After you judged the stop and the target and the USER gave their risk limit (the stop at most X% from the entry) and/or their minimum reward to risk: the highest entry worth paying (the lowest, on a short) — the entry leg's price, valid "at the level and below". Never compute it yourself; read it out. It also says the last date price traded past the stop you gave — the date for "not traded under since", never a guess.

ticker.description: The symbol — the reply also says when price last traded past the stop.

stop.description: The stop YOU judged — where the thesis breaks.

risk_limit_pct.description: The USER's risk limit: the stop at most this % from the entry, e.g. 5.

min_rr.description: The USER's minimum reward to risk at the entry, e.g. 1.5.

mentor.name: get_levels_for
mentor.description: Where the stop and the target go on THIS stock for a reward : risk the USER asked for ("I want 3:1") — measured from its own candles on the trade's scale (the horizon picks it). The stop sits past a normal pullback (the same multiple of the stock's σ over the horizon on every stock — a tighter stop is shaken out by its ordinary counter-moves), the target is the ratio × the stop; with the prices from the last close, how often that pair's target came first on its last 3 years, how long it took and how often it did not finish within the horizon's hold, and the target that FITS the horizon's time. Call it when the user names a ratio; say what the ratio COSTS on this stock in one line (e.g. "3:1 on a KO swing is a ~26% target — in the last 3 years it came first in ~2%, and 88% did not finish within the 3 months a swing holds; the target that fits a swing is ~4%"). It does not refuse a ratio and it is a description, not an edge: the stop and the target stay your judgement against the chart.

ratio.description: The reward : risk the USER asked for, as reward per 1 of risk — 3 for "3:1", 1.5 for "1.5:1".

horizon.description: The trade's horizon — it picks the scale the levels are read on (a day trade the session's 15-minute bars, a swing the daily, long term the weekly).

mentor.name: close_setup
mentor.description: Close the saved setup being edited here: its status turns to closed and the trade monitor stops watching it. It cannot be reopened. Call it only when the USER has said to close it or let it go, never on your own read that the trade is gone: say that, and ask. Saying a setup is closed without this call leaves it open.

mentor.name: remember_about_user
mentor.description:
Keep a LASTING fact about the user that they STATED, so every role knows it next time — "I never trade low-float names", "I only trade the first hour", "I hold through earnings", "call me by my first name". What you keep shows in ABOUT THE USER on every role's turns.

note.description: The fact, in a short third-person line, as the user put it: "never trades low-float names", "only trades the open". To take one back, the words of the note to remove.

forget.description: true when the user takes a fact back ("I do trade small caps now") — removes the note matching `note`.

mentor.name: consult
mentor.description:
Put ONE decision to a more capable desk head and get a straight answer back. It cannot see this conversation and cannot fetch anything — you hand it the question and every number it needs, and it thinks harder than you can in-line.

Reach for it in exactly three situations: **final sizing on real money** (live or manual — the account is at risk and the arithmetic has to be right); **two readings that genuinely disagree** and you cannot settle which one governs — most often the direction call at rung 2 of the guided build, when the structure leans one way and momentum or positioning the other and the user is waiting on your lean; and **placing a level where the structure is ambiguous** — a price that is both a prior high and a supply shelf, say. The wider-target check at rung 7 is NOT a consult: it is a tool question, answered by the levels.

Do NOT reach for it to look something up, to double-check work you are already confident in, to summarize, or because a question feels big. A consult costs a full model call and adds seconds to the turn: if you already know the answer, or a tool call would settle it, that is the cheaper and better move. Most turns should end without it.

question.description: The single decision to make, stated as a question. One decision per call — not a list, and not 'what do you think'.

context.description: Everything needed to answer it: the levels, the account size and risk rule, the two readings that disagree. The consulted desk head cannot see your conversation and cannot fetch anything, so whatever you leave out simply is not considered.

axl.name: get_trading_context
axl.description: The user's live trading venue + accounts: which modes are available (paper / live / manual), which live brokers are connected, and every account with its balance, capabilities, whether it is the SELECTED one, and the positions currently open in it. Call it before you size anything, commit to a venue, or answer any question about accounts, balances, buying power or what the user is already holding — never guess these.

axl.name: check_broker_symbol
axl.description: Check whether a specific instrument is actually TRADABLE at the user's connected live broker, and what the broker calls it (e.g. NQ → US100.cash). Three answers: tradable true (with brokerSymbol), false (the broker answered and does not list it), or null (the broker could not be reached — UNKNOWN, never treat as unavailable). Call it before recommending or building anything on a live book: a perfect setup on an instrument the broker does not list cannot be traded. Paper and manual accept anything the app can price, so this is a live-broker question.

ticker.description: The instrument to check, as the user says it e.g. AVGO, NQ, BTCUSD

axl.name: get_watched_items
axl.description: Every list the user sees in the app: setups, portfolios (as books), coverage, and the QUEUED actions waiting for a venue to open — plus, for an admin, the research queue. With status, levels and how fresh each is. This is the PLANS AND BOOKS they have made, NOT their open broker positions, balances or live P&L, which are get_trading_context. Setups and books come back scoped to the workspace the user is standing in (paper / live / manual) — those bind to an account, and merging two books into one list is not an answer. Coverage is research, binds to no account, and is shared across every workspace. Call it for "what am I watching / what have I got going / what's still open", and before saying the user has nothing. Finished items are excluded unless asked for.

kinds.description: optional — narrow to these kinds. Omit for everything, which is the usual case.

symbol.description: optional — only items on this one name e.g. NVDA

include_finished.description: include closed/finished items. Default false — finished work is history, not something being watched.

axl.name: get_performance
axl.description: The user's CLOSED-trade record: how many, win rate, net P&L, profit factor and expectancy, split by mode (paper/live/manual), by origin and by symbol. Optionally narrowed to a mode, a symbol or a date window. Win rates come back as PERCENTAGES already — never multiply them again. Use it for "how have I done", "is paper working", "what's my win rate". It reports history only; open positions and unrealized P&L are get_trading_context.

mode.description: optional — only trades in this mode. Omit to cover all of them.

symbol.description: optional — only trades on this name e.g. NVDA

axl.name: get_upcoming_events
axl.description: Dated events in a window (default the next 30 days): company earnings, Fed and macro releases, and this week's IPOs. By default scoped to the USER'S OWN names — the setups, coverage and holdings they have in the app — so the answer is about their book, not the whole market; pass scope 'market' for everything. Use it for "anything coming up", "what's the risk this week", or before discussing timing around a name they hold.

scope.description: 'mine' (default) = only the user's own names; 'market' = everything reporting in the window.

from.description: optional window start, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today.

to.description: optional window end, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to 30 days out.

axl.name: explain_concept
axl.description: A plain-language explanation of a trading concept, written for someone who has never traded — what it is, why it exists, what it costs them, and the mistake beginners make. concept.description: The term to explain, as the user said it e.g. "stop loss", "R", "drawdown", "limit order". Spelling and plurals are handled.

axl.name: set_experience_level
axl.description: Record how much trading experience this user has, so every desk knows how to talk to them. Set 'beginner' when it is clear from how they write — they ask what a basic term means, describe a goal with no mechanics, or say outright they are new. Set 'experienced' ONLY when they tell you so themselves ("talk to me normally", "I've traded for years"); you may not conclude it from jargon, and the attempt will be refused. Use 'unset' if they ask you to forget it. Pass source 'declared' when the user said it in their own words, 'inferred' when you worked it out. level.description: 'experienced' is only accepted with source 'declared' — you may not conclude it yourself.

source.description: 'declared' = the user said so in their own words. 'inferred' = you worked it out from how they write.

Call it for "what's going on today", "how are markets", "what's happening in the world", "anything I should know", and for any question about global markets, geopolitics, macro data or currencies. It is written for everyone and knows NOTHING about this user — it never mentions their positions, and you must not connect it to them either. Relay it; do not rewrite it into advice. Costs a live write when stale, so call it once per conversation unless the user asks for a refresh.

refresh.description: true to rewrite the brief instead of reading the recent one. Only when the user explicitly asks for an update.

axl.description: Whether an instrument's market is OPEN right now, and if not, exactly when it next opens. Pass `symbols` to get the industry each name is in and the house's answer for it; or `sector` (a GICS sector, e.g. Information Technology) for every sub-industry in it. echo.description: Echo's events — the house's (the intake reads earnings moves, 8-K deals, policy, defense awards, trials and news, and keeps what passes the filter: a surprise, large, more than a one-off) and the user's own — each with where it stands, its top-scored names and its flags; and the validation record so far. echo.name: map_event
echo.description: Map an event the USER names through Echo's whole pipeline — the chain (layers 1–3 both ways, losers and substitutes, every link checked against SEC filings) and the six-factor score on every link. Anything: a launch ("GTA 6 is out"), a guidance cut, a rule, a strike, a deal, a war. FRAME it first, then call once: `what_changed` (one sentence: the news, not a stock's move), `origin` (the company or country it hits directly, or the demand it moves), `tickers` (the origin's US tickers; empty for a country or a demand), `effect` (up / down / mixed: what it does to demand AT THE ORIGIN — ask the user once if unsure), `type` (demand_shock, supply_shock, policy, clinical, geopolitical, capacity_deal, confirmation), `durability` ({kind: price_spike / policy_follow_through / drug_class_shift / multi_year_commitment, why} — a locked-in commitment lasts, a price spike cures itself), `date` (YYYY-MM-DD it became public; omit for today), `size` (as a sentence, if known), `terms` (what other companies' filings call the origin).
